thread.title: Harvard expert discusses deep-sea life and global efforts to protect ocean biodiversity
thread.title_full: Harvard expert discusses deep-sea life and global efforts to protect ocean biodiversity

author: Bay State News
title: Harvard expert discusses deep-sea life and global efforts to protect ocean biodiversity
text:
Jeffrey Marlow, a biologist and author of the new book “The Dark Frontier: Unlocking the Secrets of the Deep Sea,” discussed on Apr. 14 the challenges facing deep-sea environments and ongoing international efforts to preserve marine biodiversity. Marlow, who completed postdoctoral research at Harvard’s Girguis Lab, described his experiences studying unique organisms in some of Earth’s harshest habitats and contributing to the United Nations High Seas Treaty.
Marlow said that deep-sea ecosystems are under threat from climate change, resource extraction, and overfishing. “It’s very easy to destroy these environments, and they take a very long time to come back, if they ever do,” he said. He highlighted how delicate these systems are and how human activity is beginning to have visible impacts.
During his research, Marlow explored symbiotic relationships among deep-sea creatures such as methane-eating microbes that convert greenhouse gases into rock with help from other microorganisms. He also described Osedax worms that rely on microbes inside their bodies to break down whale bones for nutrients. “We’re coming to understand more and more that life is interconnected, especially in extreme environments where there’s barely enough energy to survive on,” Marlow said.
Marlow played a role as scientific adviser for the United Nations working group behind the Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction—known as the High Seas Treaty—which took effect this January. He explained that consensus-building was key during negotiations: “They were really aiming for a treaty by consensus: It’s not that everyone is entirely happy with every word of the agreement, but rather that no one is extremely unhappy with it.” The treaty allows for creating Marine Protected Areas in international waters.
Looking ahead, Marlow expressed hope about setting aside parts of oceans for protection similar to national parks on land. “I’m excited that we as a global community can put some places in the oceans aside for protection in the same way we put aside national parks on land,” he said.
The adoption of both freedom-of-the-high-seas principles alongside common heritage values marks a shift in how humanity manages ocean resources collectively—a process Marlow finds inspiring even as many details remain unresolved.
